blindSourceSummaries: An international English-language paper (14 Apr 2025) reports the killing of a trans woman in another part of the country: she was attacked in broad daylight, the assault was filmed and the video went viral on 5 April 2025, and she died of a cardiac arrest the following afternoon; police interrogated local residents but no one was arrested, although the country's president asked authorities to investigate urgently, and events were held in several cities to denounce transphobia. Hate killed 13 trans people in the country in the first quarter of 2025, and the article recalls earlier fatal attacks (gay men lured through an app and killed, a trans rough-sleeper stabbed while sleeping, others killed in their homes or in a hairdresser). It contains no department-specific legal, enforcement or incident finding; for this record its value is national context.

An international daily (30 Jul 2024) documents armed groups in a department of the country: three armed men told a trans woman she had one week to leave town or be killed, and after hiding for a week she fled at night; 'social cleansing' flyers appeared on streets and via a messaging app naming gays, lesbians and trans women as legitimate military targets, a campaign by armed groups that is still operating. It reports eight trans women were killed in the country between February and April 2024 and 41 in 2023, and that discrimination limits trans women mainly to hairdressing or sex work. It contains no department-specific finding; the national armed-group violence, threats and displacement pattern is the claim this record relies on.

rewrites.blindSummary:
This province has no province-specific law, ordinance or incident series in the audited record; what a trans visitor here stands under is the same national framework that binds every province. A leaked draft omnibus justice package from October 2025 would enable criminal charges against LGBT people across the nation - an international rights organisation called it one of the most alarming rights rollbacks in decades - and it contains no province-specific provisions. An LGBTI+ association reported that in 2025 anti-LGBTI+ hostility became institutionalised as government policy under a 'family' banner, with senior officials' rhetoric and instructions to public institutions creating a climate encouraging rights violations.

Because the surviving record is entirely national-level and carries no provincial breakdown, neither a more protective nor a more hostile local regime can be established for this province; the documented national picture applies here unchanged.
rewrites.blindTangential: The draft package's penalties for symbolic same-sex ceremonies (up to 4 years) and the nationwide 2025 family-centred hostility campaign shape police posture toward gender-nonconforming people here as in every other province, even before the amendments are enacted.
blindSourceSummaries: An international human-rights organisation's news release (29 Oct 2025) on the leaked draft omnibus law: it would amend the national penal and civil codes to criminalise behaviour deemed 'contrary to biological sex and general morality', criminalise taking part in a same-sex engagement or marriage ceremony (penalties up to 4 years in prison), raise the minimum age for gender-affirming health care including surgery from 18 to 25 with mandatory permanent infertility, and punish health professionals who perform such care; the organisation calls it one of the most alarming rollbacks of LGBT rights in decades, and 15 national LGBT groups and the national medical association oppose the draft.

An LGBTI+ organisation's report launch on its 2025 report documents that anti-LGBTI+ hostility became institutionalised as explicit government policy, with senior officials' hate speech and instructions issued to public institutions under a 'family' banner creating a climate that encouraged human-rights violations, and regulatory/supervisory bodies systematically restricting freedom of expression and artistic freedom; the findings were presented by a lawyer at the launch.

rewrites.blindSummary: Route-3 estimate, now carrying real sub-national evidence: the largest metropolis, with a conflict-era security legacy (emergency legacies, a local guard system, high police presence). On 14 September 2024 - the day of a national anti-LGBT gathering - two men attacked two trans women with sharp objects in a district: one trans woman was killed at the scene and her friend was injured; the defendants recorded the killing and the recording entered the case file. On 19 December 2025 both were sentenced to aggravated life imprisonment for intentional killing of a woman - the strongest homicide-justice outcome in this country's record - though during the trial the national family ministry's application to intervene was accepted while the local bar association's LGBTI+ commission's was rejected, casting the government as guardian of "the family" rather than of the victim's community. Scored relative to the national score (0.15) for the country.
rewrites.blindTangential: The national family-centred hostility climate (presidency-centred; implemented through the family ministry, religious and broadcasting authorities) applies in this province as it does nationwide - a broad anti-LGBTI+ climate rather than a trans-specific local policy; no province-specific enforcement of the draft law is documented here yet.
rewrites.blindLocalsOnly: The local bar association's LGBTI+ commission's litigation role (its application was rejected in the 2025 murder trial while the family ministry's was accepted) is resident and advocate-facing, not visitor-facing.
rewrites.blindOutOfScope: General terrorism and crime advisories affect all travellers to this country regardless of identity; the 2025 draft judicial package's other measures (longer child sentences, online content removal) are not trans-specific. In this province specifically, the conflict-era security environment (emergency legacies, a local guard system, high police presence) affects everyone regardless of identity.
blindSourceSummaries: An international human-rights organisation (29 October 2025) reports a leaked draft package would amend the penal code to punish conduct 'contrary to biological sex' with up to 3 years in prison and would allow charges for anyone taking part in a same-sex engagement or marriage ceremony (up to 4 years) plus, under the civil code, raise the minimum age for gender-affirming care from 18 to 25 with a permanent-infertility mandate (providers facing fines and up to 7 years, patients up to 3 years); 15 national LGBT groups and the national medical association objected and the organisation calls for withdrawal. This is the national framework this province's record stands under; the article records no province-specific enforcement or incidents.

An LGBTI+ organisation's 2025 human rights report (published 24 February 2026) finds hostility became explicit government policy in 2025 under family-centred instructions, documenting six right-to-life violations including three hate-motivated killings with trans people most affected, 89 torture or ill-treatment violations (up from 51), and 313 right-to-liberty violations (about 2.5 times the previous year, mostly detentions); the government keeps no official hate-crime statistics, so data rely on media coverage. It is a national-level report and contains no province-specific detail.

blindSourceSummaries: A human-rights organisation's news release (29 October 2025): the leaked omnibus draft law would amend the penal and civil codes to criminalise conduct deemed "contrary to biological sex and general morality" (up to three years), sharply restrict gender-affirming healthcare (minimum age 25, onerous eligibility conditions) and allow criminal charges against both trans people and the professionals providing their care; the government's stated justification is protecting "the family" and "public morals"; the package also carries unrelated measures such as longer child sentences and online-content removal.

An online encyclopedia's country overview supplies the national framework a visitor to an interior province stands under: consensual same-sex activity has been decriminalised since the 1858 penal code, and transgender people have been able to change their legal gender since 1988, but national marriage law still gives same-sex relationships no legal recognition and offers no civil unions, domestic partnerships or joint adoption, while no comprehensive law bans discrimination on sexual orientation or gender identity and LGBTQ people are barred from open military service. It also tracks the criminalisation push the record's first source describes: in early 2026 national media reported the government was considering legislation criminalising public advocacy of 'behaviour contrary to biological sex', and that provision was ultimately not included in that year's judicial reform package; Pride events and LGBTQ gatherings were repeatedly disallowed in 2024 and 2025 with police detaining participants, per an international rights organisation. The page carries no province-specific content, so it stands only as the framework against which the record's national-score-derived model estimate for this province sits.
